records.catalog_note: Asch was born at Delft in 1603 and lived to a great age; his death date is not known. According to Houbraken he was one of the most admired artists of his day. His works are not common; examples are at Delft, Amsterdam, and Copenhagen. He is said to have worked in Wynants' and Ruisdael's manners. records.title: Portrait of an English Officer
records.catalog_note:
Beechey was born at Burford, Oxon. In 1772 he entered the Royal Academy Schools, and may have been taught there by Zoffany and Reynolds. He began to exhibit in 1776, thus being a competitor with Reynolds, Gainsborough, and Romney. From about 1783 until 1786 Beechey lived in Norwich. In 1793 he became an Associate of the Royal Academy (one year after Reynolds' death, five after Gainsborough's) and painter to the Queen. In 1798 he was elected a full member, and knighted. He continued to exhibit until his death in 1839. Portraits by Beechey are in the National Gallery, London, the Louvre, the National Portrait Gallery, London, and Kensington Palace. He is a good example of the portrait painters who revolved round Gainsborough and Reynolds.

records.title: Italian Village Scene
records.catalog_note: Jan Both was born probably in Utrecht and studied under his father, a painter on glass, and Abraham Bloemart. With his elder brother Andries he visited Italy, and his landscape is in consequence completely italianate. He was Master of the Utrecht Guild in 1649, and buried there in 1652. Both's influence was wide. He is best known for the soft golden quality of his light and atmosphere. Pictures by him are numerous in the public galleries. In the hands of the italianising Dutch painters, who having travelled in Italy then settled in Holland and continued painting more or less imaginary Italian scenes, the Dutch landscape school became conventional and mannered.

Cano practised in Seville, Madrid, and Granada, founding an academy at the latter. His earlier work is clear in tone and colour and more masculine than his later, which is smoky in colour and somewhat effeminate in type. Examples of such are in the Prado Gallery, Madrid. Alonzo died in Granada, October 5, 1667.

records.catalog_note: Claudio Coello, not to be confused with Alonzo or Juan de Coello, was born in Madrid at a date not ascertained. He studied in Italy under F. Rizi, and by copying the Venetian masters and Rubens. He  was one of Philip IV's painters, employed in the Escorial. His works, which are said to combine certain properties of Alonzo Cano, Murillo, and Velazquez, may be seen in convents in Salamanca, Saragoza, and Madrid. His chief work is the altar piece in the Sacristy of S. Lorenzo, in the Escorial. Coello, to whom the portrait below is assigned, died in 1693.
records.description:

 In type the sitter is not unlike Maria d'Este, the second wife of James II of England. A favourite painter of hers was Benedetto Gennari, to whose work this portrait bears certain resemblances. This Gennari worked in Italy and in England. A signed example of his portraiture is in the Goodwood Collection, England.

records.title: Portrait of a Nobleman
records.catalog_note: Copley was born of Anglo-Irish parents in Boston, U.S.A. He won a reputation in his native city as a portrait painter before 1774, when he left for Italy en route for England. In London in 1776 he became an Associate of the Royal Academy; in 1779 he became a full member. Before 1783 he painted his Death of Chatham and Death of Major Pierson, the former in the House of Lords, London, the latter in the National Gallery, London. In the Death of Major Pierson Copley is seen at his best- a master of pigment, an able designer, and able to express without exaggeration a certain dramatic convention. He sent  forty-three pictures to the Royal Academy, and eight to the British Institution. Copley is well represented as a portrait painter at Boston, Washington, and in the Metropolitan Museum, New York. He died in London, September 9, 1815
records.catalog_title: Ascribed to Copley.  No. 9. PORTRAIT OF A NOBLEMAN
records.description:
Half length standing, nearly full face, in scarlet and ermine robes. His left arm draped with heavy folds of white silk and ermine is akimbo, against the sky. The right is extended right across the canvas to the left, the hand hanging over the edge of a rock. A pillar on the left background and one in the centre, behind the head; to left and right, beyond, tree stems and foliage against a sky of singularly rich egg-blue. An orange glow low down on the right.

 Formerly in St. George's Hall, Easton-in-Gordano, N. Somersetshire, England. Though traditionally attributed to Copley, this portrait does not satisfactorily tally with his style. It is clearly influenced by Reynolds, and is nearer Hoppner than Copley. It was formerly called The Earl of Chatham, for whom it is much too young.

records.catalog_note:
Michael Dahl was a Swedish portrait painter, trained in France and Italy, and practising in England. Born in 1659 he came to England soon after Lely's death (1680); then went to France and Rome, returning to England in 1688. He quickly gained a reputation and became a serious rival to Sir Godfrey Kneller. He painted Queen Anne and Prince George of Denmark, and had a large practice among the aristocratic class.  His masterpiece is his Sir Cloudesley Shovell, the famous admiral, painted about 1702, and now in the Painted Hall, Greenwich, England. His Queen Anne as Princess is in the National Portrait Gallery, London, where too are other pieces by him. At his best Dahl was a capable and accomplished painter. Living to a great age (d. 1743) he produced inferior work after 1735.

 See C. H. Collins Baker: Lely and the Stuart Portrait Painters. London. 1912

records.title: The Philosopher; or Saint Jerome in his Study
records.catalog_note: This type of picture originating in Quinten Massys (1466-1530) represents the birth of the early XVIth Century genre in the Netherlands, as opposed to religioius paintings.  Beginning with these comparatively serious themes - philosophers sitting in secluded contemplation of our inevitable lot while the world passes on its careless way outside, Flemish and Dutch genre quickly introduced a more amusing kind of subject, culminating in the XVIIth or early XVIIIth Century version of the Reymerswael and Massys type of philopsphers.  There are many versions of it, one in the Jhnson Collection, Philadelphia.  One is known bearing the monogram of Jan Massys.
records.catalog_title: No. 12. THE PHILOSOPHER, or ST. JEROME IN HIS STUDY
records.description:
An elderly grey bearded man, in a deep vermilion robe, seated behind a table, his head resting on his right hand, his left forefinger on the temple of a skull. Before him on the left his reading desk with an open book thereon, illuminated with an Ascension. On a lower shelf of the desk two books, one inscribed MCCCVI, another PAULI XV. On the left a crucifix, a window with round leaded glass, and an iris in a pot. Towards the right on the table a pair of snuffers, a guttered candle in a brass stick, a scarlet hour glass, and four volumes. An open window in the background gives on to a distant village with figures and horses and distant rocky hills.

 Formerly attributed to Quinten Massys.

 NOTE TO No. 12.
 This painting was purchased from Martin Colnaghi, who, during the better part of his life, had made a special study of the works of the early Low Countries painters, and was regarded as an authority whose opinion was worthy of consideration. He sold this for a work by Quinten Massys, and in positive terms to the writer confirmed this statement, which since has been sustained by several well-known experts. R.C.H.

records.title: Artemisia Drinking the Ashes of Mausolus
records.catalog_title: No. 14. ARTEMISIA DRINKING THE ASHESOF MAUSOLUS
records.description:
Seated with upturned face, three-quarters length, three-quarters to the right. In her right hand she raises the goblet containing her husband's ashes steeped in water. To the right a stone inscribed [in Greek].

 Artemisia, Queen of Caria, wife and sister of Mausolus (who died B.C. 353), was so devoted to him that she mixed his ashes with water and drank them off. Then she had a monument designed and built to his memory.  This " mausoleum " was accounted one of the seven wonders of the world. Scopas,Timotheus, Leochares, Bruxis, and Pithis, the greatest architects of the day, were all engaged on the work. The ruins of this, the original mausoleum, exist near Budrum. The above picture is by a painter derived from the Rubens atelier; possibly one of the practically unknown pupils of Jordaens.

records.catalog_note: The finest qualities of the minor German masters of the early XVIth Century are typified in the Portrait of a Man, possibly by Bartholomew Bruyn. Acquired at the last moment, this picture takes its proper place with the most important examples in the Memorial. (1913 Catalogue preface, p vi)
records.description:
Head and shoulders, seen against a pale blue sky and mountain distance. He wears a black velvet doublet, with a red silk lining, his hands are clasped before him.

 Hans Muelich and with more probability Bartholomaeus Bruyn have been suggested as the painters of this refined and masterly portrait. This period (early XVIth Century) of German Portraiture has not been satisfactorily explored. The name of Christopher Amberger is generally used, more or less generically,
 to cover numerous portraits whose common trait is an ascetic culture and refinement. Ludger to Ring is another master of this somewhat obscure period. His masterpiece perhaps is at present on loan in the Metropolitan Museum, New York. Another master is Barthel Beham. The picture in this Collection is among this class of sensitively refined and drawn portraits; others are in the Johnson Collection, Philadelphia.

records.title: English Landscape
records.catalog_note: Ibbetson was born in Yorkshire and apprenticed to a ship painter of Hull. He also painted scenery for "The Genii," a play performed in York and Hull. He went to London in 1777, there painting landscape, cattle and country people. He worked in obscurity till about 1785, when he began to exhibit. In 1788 Ibbetson was chosen as draughtsman to accompany Colonel Cathcart's embassy to China. On the voyage he gained some knowledge of ships and the sea, and immediately returned to London. His first wife's death in 1794, added to financial worries, undermined his health, and he retired to the country. He remarried in 1801. In 1803 he published An Accidence or Gamut of Painting in Oil (2nd edition, with a memoir, published 1828). He died 1817, at Masham, Yorkshire, his native place. After his death a volume of his etchings was published. Ibbetson, who is at his best a painter of considerable accomplishment and individual charm, is represented in the National Gallery and the Victoria and Albert Museum, London. His works are marked by a pleasant silvery atmosphere.

records.catalog_note: Maria Angelica Kauffmann was born at Coire, and taught by her father. Her precocity in music, languages, and painting is said to have been great. In 1754 her family took her to Milan, where she copied the masters. In 1759 she was in Rome, there painting portraits and attracting much attention. She went to Venice 1764 and thence in 1765 to England. There she was elected a foundation member of the Royal Academy. She is one of two cases, if not the unique instance, of a woman being member of the Royal Academy. She was unlucky in love, marrying a polygamist valet whom she mistook for his master.  She had to pay out some L300 before she was relieved of him. Then she married Zucchi, an Italian painter and Associate of the Royal Academy. With him she returned to Italy. Angelica has the reputation of having been one of the most charming and accomplished women of her day; her social success in London was prodigious. Reynolds painted her twice. She died in Rome, 1807; pictures by her are in the Berlin, Dresden, Munich, St. Petersburg, and Vienna Galleries.
records.catalog_title: No. 21. ZEUXIS SELECTING MODELS FOR HIS PICTURE OF HELEN OF TROY
records.description:
Zeuxis is seated in the right centre profle left. Before him stands a woman turned to the right, and looking down to the left front. The painter holds her right arm, her left is raised holding a drapery. Further to the left sits a woman with a white robe round her waist unfastening her left sandal. Her torso is bare, and she looks towards Zeuxis. Two more women stand on the left, one with her back to the spectator, looking out of the picture to the left. On the right by Zeuxis' painting table a girl picking up a brush. A large clean canvas in the right background. Signed "Angelica Kauffmann Pinx."

 An admirable example of late XVIIIth Century classicism. Zeuxis, the best known of the Greek painters, but not the peer of the greatest, flourished about 468 B.C. He painted a picture of Helen of Troy, afterwards placed in the temple of Juno Lacinia, in Italy. This he painted for the people of Crotona who accommodated him with the choicest of their maidens for models. Zeuxis, like Paris in the celebrated Judgment, had to select the most beautifully formed of these girls, and ultimately retained five. In the above picture his models are preparing for a sitting. The fine spirit of the Crotonans, who were proud that their virgins should be the material for the great artist's inspiration, was echoed during the French Revolution, when it was a matter of emulation and great honour that the girls of the best standing in Paris should pose naked for Louis David's classic pictures.

records.title: Anne King, Countess of Waldegrave
records.catalog_note: Born at Bristol Lawrence was by 1780 working as a pastel portrait painter at Oxford. Then he set up in Bath, and in 1787 moved to London, and entered the Royal Academy Schools. In 1791, too young to be a regular Associate of the Academy, he was made a Supplemental Associate. Reynolds dying in 1792, Lawrence succeeded him as painter in ordinary to the King. In 1794 he was a Royal Academician. Between 1787 and 1830 he sent 311 pictures to the Academy. His best pictures, such as Miss Farren (Pierpont Morgan Collection) and F. Angerstein and his Wife (Louvre), and the Bathurst portraits are brilliantly attractive. His pencil drawings are remarkable for honesty of handling and sympathy of interpretation. But Lawrence succeeded too well; he was the typical popular Academician, who threw off commissions, in which he felt no interest, with no effort and at no cost. In consequence he was knighted and medalled to the top of his bent. As a collector of masters' drawings Lawrence is known to have shown fine taste; his collection was unequalled. He is about the last of the prominent painters who in the great private English galleries carried on the line of portraits started in Elizabeth's reign. With Lawrence this line breaks, and is only intermittently taken up by isolated portraits; photographs fill in the gaps. Lawrence, who succeeded West as P.R.A. in 1820, died in 1830.

records.catalog_note: Paolo de Matteis, or Matthei, was born at Cilento, and studied under that clever technician Luca Giordano and G. M. Morandi. He worked in Rome for Clement XI and XII and for Benedict XIII. He lived for three years in France, gaining great repute. Many of his works are in Genoa and Naples and at Monte Cassino, where he worked in 1692 and 1706-9. He died in Naples, 1728.

records.title: Pope Innocent X (after Velazquez)
records.catalog_note:
Born in Madrid presumably about 1600, del Mazo entered Velazquez' studio when quite young and remained until the master's death (1660). In 1634 he married Velazquez' daughter, and in 1660 succeeded to his office as Court painter. He died in 1667. From the few signed examples of his work that are known he can be put down as a skilled reproducer of the external qualities of Velazquez' painting. In the inner properties, such as crisp unerring draughtsmanship, peculiar beauty of texture, intimate and unreproducible mastery of pigment, and above all in human understanding, del Mazo does not pretend to compete with his master. Yet such was his training and, we must recognise, his adaptability that were no single example of Velazquez' mature work extant del Mazo would take rank as an unusual master. The portraits such as the Innocent X in this Collection, usually assigned to him, are inevitably judged by a superlatively exacting standard; and in that comparison del Mazo suffers. But if, for example, the Doria Palace and Hermitage portraits of Innocent  were destroyed we should be able from del Mazo's copies to form a better idea of Velazquez than we could in similar circumstances form of any other painter. As things are, however, "every portrait by del Mazo, in the Prado and elsewhere, is stamped as a secondhand Velazquez." His best picture is generally said to be the Don Tiburcio y Cruzat
 in the Prado; he also painted landscape and sea pieces.
 See C. G. Hartley: Spanish Painting. 1904.

records.catalog_note:
With barely an exception the Milanese painters capitulated to the Florentine Leonardo da Vinci, and abandoning the old traditions of their school as exemplified by Vincenzo Foppa, one and all essayed to catch the wonderful mystery, the incommunicable spirit of Leonardo's types. The famous Virgin of
 the Rocks and the yet more famous Mona Lisa are typical of the elusive, haunting meaning that baffled all Leonardo's followers. The purity of his sense of form and this incommunicable mystery became under a Luini and Solario sweetened and mannered; the beautiful became the suavely pretty, the elusive became obvious. Other followers of Leonardo at Milan were Cesare da Cesto, Salaino, Leonardo's favourite pupil, Pedrini, Melzi, Ambrozio di Predis, and Marco d'Oggiono. Solario, in whose manner is the picture described below, is best seen in Milan, London, Berlin, and Paris. Two examples are in the Johnson Collection, Philadelphia.

records.catalog_note:
Antonis Mor, or Antonio Moro, was born in Utrecht, and studied under Jan van Scorel. According to Van Mander he went early to Rome. In 1547 he was in the Guild at Utrecht. His first important patron was Cardinal Granvelle, who took him to Brussels in 1548. Two years later Mor was again in Rome; thence he was sent to Madrid by Mary of Hungary, and on to Lisbon to paint Dona Maria, the Portuguese king's sister. For a while Mor passed about between Rome, Genoa, and Madrid, and in 1552 went into England to paint Queen Mary. He stayed perhaps a year, then returning to the Netherlands. He was now constantly employed by Philip II of Spain and by Margaret of Parma. Mor died in Antwerp in 1576. His best portraits are in the Prado, at Cassel, Vienna, and Brussels. There is a fine Alva by him in the Huntingdon Collection, New York. Such portraits prove him to have been a master not un- worthy of comparison with Holbein.
 See Henri Hymans: Antonio Moro. 191O.
records.catalog_title: No. 29. PORTRAIT OF AN UNKNOWN LADY
records.description:
Half length, standing, facing slightly to the left. Dressed in black with brocaded dark crimson sleeves from the elbow to the wrist. Round her waist a heavy gold chain with circular fluted links. Two rings on each forefinger, one on the left forefinger a plain gold circlet. Two rings set with large stones on the third finger of the left hand, one on the little finger of the right; the right hand rests on a brown covered table in the left corner. She wears a white pleated yoke and is coiffee de la cornette. A large pearl drop is fastened inside her coif; a large ruby, the centre of a star of eight pearls, hangs on her breast. Dark brown background.

 The solid bars in the chain round the waist are decorated with fleur de lys, perhaps indicating that the wearer is of the French Royal House. In general appearance she resembles the Dona Fuana in the Prado, Madrid, more closely than any other portrait by Mor. The portrait in this Collection was formerly described as Queen Mary; it bears however no resemblance to her. A photograph of the picture, thus described was submitted to Henri Hymans, who rightly rejected the name of Queen Mary. Without examining the painting the eminent critic dismissed the attribution to Mor as well. In the opinion of the present writer M. Hymans would have reconsidered his verdict had he had an opportunity of judging the portrait by the original.

records.title: Itinerant Musician
records.catalog_note: Adriaen, the elder brother and instructor of Isack van Ostade, was born at and lived in Haarlem all his life. His first master was Frans Hals, whose influence is not strongly reflected in his work. His earlier pieces represent scenes of drinking and dancing, and introduce effects of sudden, even crude lighting and violent action. In these early works he painted many figures. After 1640 his pictures become more reticent and harmonious, with subtle effects of tone, fewer even single figures. He also attempted some out-of-doors pieces and a few portraits. From about 1647 to 1670 he was at his best. Later his painting became small and polished in execution and in colour rather gaudy. He is admirably represented in Amsterdam, Berlin, London, The Hague, Paris, Dresden, and Vienna. A. van Ostade died in Haarlem 1685. His brother Isack, a painter of rare charm, died when only twenty-eight; his earliest work is often confused with that of Adriaen.
records.description:
An elderly man, his body profile to the right his head bent down, full face standing at half length. He wears a brown hat with a green plume, a bottle green coat and dull plum-coloured cape hanging behind him. His right arm stretched across his body; in the hand the handle of a hurdy-gurdy.

records.title: The Holy Family with St. Elizabeth and St. John the Baptist
records.catalog_note:
Rubens was born at Siegen, in Westphalia, and first studied under Tobias Verhaagt and Adam van Noort. Later he went to Otho van Veen. In 1600 he went to Italy, there staying till 1608. Then he returned to Antwerp and became Court painter to the Regents of the Netherlands; in 1609 he married Isabella Brant. At this time Rubens developed an enormous business in Antwerp; his studio, or workshop, was filled with students and assistants (Van Dyck among them), who were ceaselessly engaged in carrying out his designs. In 1621 in Paris he was commissioned by Marie de Medici to paint a series of great canvases, celebrating her career, for the new palace of the Luxembourg. In 1628 he was sent to Madrid, where he met the young Velazquez. Next year another mission took Rubens to England, where he was knighted. His first wife had died, and in 1630 he married her niece, Helene Fourment, the sister of Susanne Fourment, whose portrait is the famous Chapean de Paille in the London Gallery. At this time he was fifty-three, Helene little more than a girl. His happy and prolific union gave Rubens a fresh impetus; his art responded to his own physical joie de vivre, and in the last years of his life he produced some of his masterpieces of sensuous colour and forms. Ele built a palatial house in Antwerp, and spent the summers in his Chateau de Steen. The victim of gout, he died in 1640. Rubens was a painter who immediately responded to his physical emotions. Thus his two periods of married life are marked in his art by work of ardently sensuous expressions, by a zest for violent action, for voluptuous form and colour. The sensual appeal of his work is so primal and candid as to be free from any meretricious flavour. But he cannot be ranked with the penetrative seers; he was too successful and too physical to be a revealer of immaterial things. On the other hand he is one of the supreme masters of design, draughtsmanship and paint. His influence in Italy, the Netherlands, France and in the best schools of to-day was and remains powerful.

 See Max Rooses: L'Oeuvre de Rubens. 5 vols. 1886-1892. (Translated by Harold Child, 2 vols.); Bode: Dutch and Flemish Painters. 1911
records.catalog_title: No. 40. THE HOLY FAMILY WITH ST ELIZABETH AND ST. JOHN BAPTIST
records.description:
The Virgin seated in the centre looking down to the right front, holding the Child with both hands. He stands on her deep blue mantle, on a parapet, looking down and extending his left hand to the child St.  John, who sits on the right profile left, on St. Elizabeth's knee. He is quite naked; the child Christ has a fold of linen round His waist. St. Elizabeth is seated profile left on the right, dressed in a smoke-grey hood and mantle, with a gold coloured band over her forehead; in her lap, under St. John, is his furry pelt. The Virgin is dressed in a clear vermilion tunic, a blue-grey hood, and deep steel-blue mantle. Behind her on the left, looking over the Christ's head, stands St. Joseph, in a deep bottle-green mantle. The flesh tone of the Virgin's and St. Elizabeth's heads, and of the two children is conspicuously blond and luminous. The light shimmers on the little St. John's flaxen hair and gold-ivorine flesh. A remarkable rendering is made of refracted light beating up on the Virgin's face.

 A slightly differing version of this Holy Family, by Rubens, is in the Wallace Collection, London. It was painted in 1616-17 for the Archduke Albert Co-Regent of the Netherlands, and is alluded to in Max Rooses' great work on the master. Critical analysis of these two pictures proves that the Wallace Collection panel (same dimensions) is the earlier. The Providence picture shows that it originally had the necklace round the Christ's neck and the loose wisps of hair falling across Mary's forehead and cheek, that are seen in the London piece; but by an afterthought they were removed. Other differences occur, such as the size and tone of the Virgin's neck, which is larger and more disturbing in the Wallace Gallery picture; the fulness of the Christ's left cheekbone, in the London example, has been corrected in the panel in this Memorial, and the correction is clearly visible; the Christ in the Providence version has a little linen wrap over His waist; this may be a later addition, not by the master; the Wallace Christ has no drapery. The Wallace Collection St. Elizabeth's drapery is a warmer grey. In the Wallace Gallery example St. Joseph is stretching his left arm across the picture, behind the Blessed Virgin. As regards execution the London picture is crisper and more spontaneous in brushwork, as is natural in a first conception. The picture in this Collection came from the Sciarra Colonna Gallery in Rome.

records.title: The Holy Family
records.provenance: The version in this Memorial was formerly in the Erle Drax, Olantigh Towers Collection. Sold at Christie's, 191O.
records.catalog_note: Andrea d'Agnolo the Faultless (see Browning's Andrea Del Sarto) was born in Florence, and taught by Piero di Cosimo. He also studied the frescoes of Masaccio and Ghirlandaio, and the cartoons of Michelangelo and Leonardo. Then he entered in a partnership with Franciabigio, with him working in the Piazza del Grano. He also at this time decorated the Cortile of the Scalzi. In 1515-16 Andrea was invited to France by Francis I; he stayed there a year, and then returned ostensibly to fetch his wife Lucrezia and to buy pictures for Francis I. But through some laxity of moral fibre, some quality correspondent with his easy and effortless work, he fell to misappropriating Francis' money; spending it on his wife and her friends. Not of the strong stuff from which successful criminals are made, Andrea succumbed to remorse. His wife deserted him; he was driven to hack work, and at last died of plague in 1531. His works are in most of the great galleries.
records.description:
The Virgin, St. Elizabeth, and the Holy Children; four figures. Mary kneels on the left holding the Christ to her with her left hand. Her right lies on her knee. Her hood is deep rose shot with viridian-green; her bodice rose-red with golden undersleeves, her shawl bronze-grey, her skirt mossgreen. The Christ stands against her His right knee raised, His left hand on her breast. He looks round to the right at St. John, who stands profile left with crossed legs, holding up and pointing with his right hand. St. Elizabeth coiffed in white is behind him enfolding him with both hands; a pelt of copper-coloured fur round his waist. St. Elizabeth wears a dark plum-brown tunic under her white hood and shawl. The Christ has a gauze-like cambric cloth round His loins and held in His left hand.

 Painted after 1516. There are three known variants of this Holy Family. One in the Louvre with six figures; one at Munich with five figures and apparently the traces of a sixth head, and a repetition or copy of the Munich piece in Vienna. The example in the Annmary Brown Memorial differs in detail and in design from the Louvre and Munich pieces. It is closer to the Munich than to the Louvre example, but yet differs not only in having four instead of five figures, but also the following details. In the Providence example the Christ has a lawn drapery, in the Munich piece none; St. Elizabeth's hood is more fringed in the Munich picture and the folds at the back of her head are different. The Christ's head is tilted further back in the Munich example; the feet of St. John in the Munich piece differ in pose, his pelt is different, and in the Providence picture Mary has no lock of hair falling over her jaw on to her neck. Andrea painted numerous Holy Families; differing examples are in the Pitti, Florence, the Wallace Collection and the National Gallery, London, and in the Hermitage. The version in this Memorial was formerly in the Erle Drax, Olantigh Towers Collection. Sold at Christie's, 191O.

 Note to No. 41:
 Of this subject, Mary, the infant Jesus, St. Elizabeth and St. John by Del Sarto, there are known to be eight.  That in the Pitti is possibly the first and probably the only one in which his wife does not seem to appear as having posed for the Mother of Jesus.  The others, in which she is seen to have been the model for the Virgin, are in the Wallace Collection; Hermitage, St. Petersburg; Old Pinakothek, Munich; National Gallery, London; two in the Louvre, paris; and Annmary Brown memorial.  In each the dominant motive is the Virgin Mary, Jesus, St. Elizabeth, and St. John.  They are always in the centre foreground and never twice posed alike.  For this reason it may be said of them that neither is a copy of another; but that all, to a certain extent, are original as to composition, and several vary as to number of attending figures.  In official catalogues all, without reservation, are attributed to Del Sarto.
 R.C.H.

records.title: The Circumcision
records.catalog_note: Born near Naples and at first taught by his father, Angelo Solimena, Francesco was sent to Naples in 1674 to work under Francesco di Maria. From him he passed to Giacomo del Po. Later he went to Rome, emulating there the works of P. da Cortona, Lanfranco and Guido. In time Solimena became himself a model to the rising generation. He, as well as P. da Cortona, Guido, and the rest, was the admired objective of the French students who in the XVIIIth Century were sent to Rome to acquire the grand style. Solimena's best works are at Naples; others are in Dresden, Milan, Paris and Rome. In 1702 he was commissioned by Philip V of Spain to paint pictures for the Royal Chapel, Madrid. Dying in Naples, 1747, at the age of ninety, Solimena bequeathed a large school of imitators. To Solimena, Sebastiano Conca and the other Neapolitans is due the especial significance now attached to the term Neapolitan. By the word we understand a school of chiaroscurists who, while conventional and mannered and almost wholly divorced from real life, were yet considerable masters of the brush. The example described below is in this way typical of the Neapolitan XVIIth and XVIIIth Century School.
records.description: The Babe is laid on an altar high up in the centre, supported by the high priest on the left. The Mother kneels on the left, below, in a blue-green mantle and grey-gold hood and shawl. To the right, on the top altar step, stands an attendant, profile left in yellow, holding a torch. In the fore- ground another mother, nursing her child, descending the altar steps. A half naked beggar in the left corner. In the centre two doves, brought as an offering.

records.title: Adoration of the Magi
records.description:
Mary is seated on the right, full length three-quarters to the left, holding her Son naked on her right knee. She is dressed in dark brown-red and Antwerp blue. The little Christ is seated three-quarters left, raising His right hand in blessing.  Before Mary, kissing the Infant's right foot, kneels Melchior, the oldest of the Kings, in ermine and vermilion. A chalice, his gift, and his green cap, are in the paved court below Mary. Immediately above Melchior stands Balthasar, a gold cup in his left hand, his right arm in its rich golden sleeve held up across his body. He looks to the left, where stands Jaspar, the African King of Saba, in profile right, also bearing a gold chalice in his right hand.  In the background a ruined archway, rocks on the left, and distant mountains in the centre and on the right. Behind Mary a vermilion curtain with an effect of sunlight and shadow; the Star above her head.

 This is by a painter of the XVIth Century Flemish School. The type of the Virgin and of the Child suggest that the artist was Spanish. On the other hand, the influence of Quentin Massys and in especial of Mabuse is very strong. A somewhat similar picture showing the same prevailing influences is in the
 National Gallery, London, inscribed " Lo Fil De Mestre Rodriguez." The influence of Mabuse was very much felt in Spain and Portugal in the XVIth Century.

records.title: A Scene from Roman History
records.catalog_note: Born 1550, in Steenwijck, H. van Steenwijck the elder was pupil to J. de Vries, a painter of perspectives. Steenwijck followed him in this style. He was in especial fond of painting torchlight scenes. The Franckens usually introduced the figures in his pictures. Steenwijck was the master of P. Needs (see No. 33). He died about 1604. His pictures are in the Galleries at Amsterdam, Brussels, London, and Vienna. The picture below attributed to him somewhat resembles the picture in the National Gallery, London.
records.catalog_title: Attributed to Steenwijck. No. 45. A SCENE FROM ROMAN HISTORY
records.description:
The interior of a Renaissance palace, a marble- paved bed chamber with a green-canopied golden couch to the right, an aged king lying on it. At the foot of the couch a Roman in a toga stands with his back to the spectator addressing the king and pointing to the left background, where a centurion appears mounting a flight of stairs. The balustrade is of white stone with red marble pilasters; an orange tree in a bronze pot stands on the balus- trade; beyond a sphinx on a pedestal. An archway and distant door beyond. Sunlight falls on the background and across the foreground on the white and dull-rose marble flags. In the left foreground a Roman soldier carrying a tray with a small vessel on it. Above his head in the background a picture, apparently of a holy family. Signed " H. v. S . . . jk."

 The figures in this painting are clearly less delicate in handling, and are the work of a collaborator, possibly one of the Franckens.

records.title: Benjamin West, P.R.A.
records.provenance: Sir Walter Gilbey Collection, sold at Christie's  1910.
records.catalog_note: Stuart was born in Narraganset, Rhode Island. He was taught by a Scottish painter-Alexander, of Newport, who took him to Scotland. Returning to America, he settled in Boston and then New York. Finding, however, imperfect encouragement Stuart in 1778 set sail for England. After a period of desultory occupations he became Benjamin West's pupil in 1780.  At length he began to practise independently. In 1786 he married, and about 1788 went to Dublin, where he had great success. In 1793 he returned to America, stopping in New York and going on to Philadelphia, where he painted Washington. Portraits and repetitions of " the Father of Freedom " by and after Stuart abound. In a general way they do not represent his best work. Stuart moved subsequently to Washington and in 1806 to Boston, where he died in 1828. He was a brilliant conversationalist and skilled musician. As a portrait painter he atones for technical deficiencies with a curiously individual way of seeing his sitters. He is represented in Boston, Washington, New York, the National Portrait Gallery (where some of his best work is) and National Gallery, London, and at Yale University.
records.description:

records.title: Mater Dolorosa
records.catalog_note: Born in Bologna, and studying there for some time, Tiarini at length had to flee to Florence because of a quarrel. In Florence he worked under Passignano. Athome meanwhile the eclectic Carracci had become famous and Tiarini plucked up heart and returned. He soon gained a name, and painted Mary Magdalene and La Madonna Addolorata with conspicuous success.  His principal works are The Virgin, Mary Magdalerze, and St. John weeping over the Passion lnstruments in S. Benedetto, Bologna, St. Catherine before a Crucifix in S. Maria Maddalene, and St. Dominic restoring the dead Child in S. Dominic, Bologna. There is much in common between Guido Reni and Tiarini, who died at Bologna 1668.

records.title: The Assumption of the Virgin
records.catalog_note:
Tiepolo, one of the last great Venetian masters, was born in Venice, and studied under Lazzarini. The influence of Paolo Veronese and of that brilliant virtuoso, Piazzetta, are traceable in him. He married Guardi's sister in 1715. Till about 1740 Tiepolo was busy in and round Venice; he decorated the churches and the great palazza and villas. In 1750 he went to Wurtzburg to adorn the Archbishop's palace, returning to Venice in 1753. In 1755 he was elected Director of the Venice Academy; in 1762 he resigned and went at the Spanish king's invitation to Madrid to decorate the Royal Palace. His reception was magnificent, and his hands were filled with commissions. He died in Madrid, 1770. Venetian art may be said to have come to a brilliant end with Tiepolo and Guardi. The fervent piety of the Venetian School under Bellini had died out two hundred years before Tiepolo. In its place the sumptuous exuberance of colour, design and physical well-being initiated by Giorgione had run for two centuries and a half, expressed by Titian, Palma, Tintorett, Paolo Veronese, and lastly Tiepolo. He summed up and crystallised, in terms of his own day, the essence of the late Renaissance in Venice.

 See Fransz Hermann Meissner: Tietolo. Leipzig, 1897. E. March Phillips: The Venetian School. 1912

records.description: In the centre, towards the zenith, the Blessed Virgin seated on clouds, gazing upwards, with out- spread arms. She is clad in white and blue. Above her a cherubim descending, pointing upwards with his left arm; another supports the Virgin's left arm. Below her is an angel, in rose-red, with blue and white pinions, seated on clouds, looking upwards with his right arm outstretched.

records.title: George Washington
records.catalog_note: John Trumbull, born in Lebanon 1756, entered the Army in 1775. He seems to have had a firm liking for drawing from his earliest days. In 1777, resigning his commission, he returned to Boston and to painting.  He took Smibert's painting room and copied some of his works; but finding no one in Boston capable of helping him, and yet hankering after a military life, he volunteered as an aide to General Sullivan, with whom he served in the Rhode Island campaign of 1778. Then he returned to Boston, and in 1780 sailed for Europe. By way of Paris he went to England. He was arrested after Major Andre's death, but well treated. Through Benjamin West's aid he was at length freed; he had meanwhile copied a Correggio. Returning to America Trumbull made up his mind to take up painting as a profession and again sailed for London, arriving 1784. His pictures  appeared from 1786 (Bunker's Hill). Back in America in 1789 Trumbull stayed here till 1794, then going on diplomatic work to England. There he painted during 1808-1815. In 1817 he was decorating the Capitol, Washington. He was president of the Academy, New York. Most of Trumbull's pictures are at Yale. He died 1843.
records.catalog_title: Attributed to Trumbull. No. 49. GEORGE WASHINGTON
records.description:
Bust portrait, the head three-quarters left, the body square to the front. Dark blue-green uniform gold epaulettes, gold-grey lapels and collar, and white stock. The hair is powdered grey, the chin  slightly raised. Four buttons seen on his coat. Grey background. Signed " 1776, J. T."

 In Trumbull's Autobiography a list is given of pictures painted before 1780, before the painter had had any instruction. On this list occurs a portrait of General Washington; done from memory of another picture by Peale. He held an exhibition in New York before he left for England; No. 57 in the catalogue was " Washington, half length, from memory." The picture described above has been traditionally identified with this No. 57, which, after the sale of 1780, was lost sight of. An engraving by Blanchard- "dessine par Conder " -resembles this portrait.

 A label, said to be inscribed in Trumbull's writing and formerly affixed to this portrait, bears this legend: "Life-size bust portrait of Gen. Washington in 1776. Exhib. in N. York and admired very much. taken by me to England, had to hide it away with my friend)  B.W.-J.T."

records.title: Marriage of Saint Catherine
records.catalog_note: The picture below has been attributed to the some- what vague, generic painter Bonifazio. At one time three Bonifazi were assumed; lately but one is permitted by the most expert authorities. The picture in question is in the nature of a pasticcio of Titian. The little St. John is derived from the Madonna with the Cherries at Vienna, the Madonna and St. Catherine from the Virgin and Child with Four Saints at Dresden. The Child, seated on His mother's hand and leaning forward, recalls Bonifazio's Adoration of the Magi in the Accademia, Venice.
records.description: The Virgin is seated on the left, three-quarters length, three-quarters to the right; her head is bowed to the right. She wears a golden-brown hood, vermilion tunic, and deep mulberry cloak. On the left the boy St. John, seen only to the shoulders, looks up, profile right, holding out in his right hand a scroll inscribed " Ecce agnus." The Virgin holds with her two hands the little Christ, who leans forward in a sitting posture and places the ring on St. Catherine's right hand. She stands on the right profile left with bent head. Deep blue sky in the right and centre background; a dull red hanging on the left.

records.title: A Bay on the Mediterranean
records.catalog_note:
Claude Vernet, commonly called Joseph Vernet, was born at Avignon, and taught by his father Antoine Vernet and Adrian Manglard. In 1732 Joseph went to Italy meaning to adopt historical painting, but the charm of the Mediterranean captivated him, and he became a painter of landscape and port scenes. But for a short visit to Greece he remained in Italy for twenty years, most of the time in poverty; he is said to have exchanged his pictures for old suits of clothes. But in time he won his way, and such was his repute by 1750 that Louis V invited him to Paris. The next year he was admitted to the Academie and commissioned to paint a set of about twenty French seaports. After ten years he had done fifteen; wearied by the mechanical nature of his commission he threw it up. He died in Paris 1789. His son was Carl Vernet, his grandson Horace, the well-known battle painter, whose canvases abound at Versailles. Joseph Vernet and Zuccarelli between them established a numerous school of Italian landscapists; the picture described below is of Vernet's School.
 See P. M. Turner and C. H. Collins Baker: Stories of the French artists. 1909.

records.title: British Commerce
records.dimensions: 19 1/2 in. h. by 24 3/4 in. w, oval
records.provenance: Sir Walter Gibley Collection ; obtained at Christie's in 1910
records.catalog_note:
West was born in Chester County, Pennsylvania. It seems that at eight years old he was taught by Cherokee Indians; later he moved to Philadelphia and New York, in both painting portraits. Making money thus, and assisted by good friends, he was able to go to Rome in 1760. He was a social success and remained in Italy three years, visiting Florence, Bologna, Venice, and Parma. In 1763 he arrived in London, where his reception was so promising that he sent home for his fiancee, and settled finally in England.  He painted many pictures of sacred and profane history. His main contribution to art lies in his having painted English soldiers dressed in uniform instead of classical Roman costume. In 1768 he was
 one of four commissioners appointed to frame the constitution of the Royal Academy, and in 1772 was made historical painter to the King; he designed decorations for Windsor Castle. He succeeded Reynolds as P.R.A., but being a Quaker refused knighthood. West died in 1820 and was buried in St. Paul's. His Death of Wolfe is in Grosvenor House, London.
records.description:
Britannia is seated to the right, profile left. Behind her her shield, in her right hand a winged sceptre ending in an oar blade to denote naval dominion.  Three maidens attendant by her, represent the arts of sculpture, architecture, and painting. In the centre putti receiving the riches of the East and Mediterranean that are laid at Britannia's feet. On the left stand an Indian chief, a Hindu woman, and a woman representing America, with hands outstretched. Behind her on the left a figure carrying a box. Sea with frigates in the centre distance. Signed " B. West, 1791."

 Exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1791 with a pendant sketch, " British Manufactory."
records.references:

records.title: A Morning with Parini
records.description:
A Venetian interior. In the left centre a woman in brocaded dress and rose-pink mantle, leaning back in a gold silk chair. Behind her a man in a white peruque, seated with his left arm on the chair back. On the left, by a fireplace in the background, Parini stands in black, declaiming from one of his Odi or his Giorno. A background of gold fluted pillars, a mirror in the centre. Signed  " G. Barbaglia."

 A brilliant example of modern "impressionistic " painting, shimmering with the sense of light and circulating air. Parini (1729-99) was a reformer of Italian poetry. He lived in and taught literature at Milan. His models were Pope and Thomson. His masterpiece is the Giorno (1763-65), translated into English as A Fashionable Day. In this he whips with subtle irony the fops of his Milan. His works were published by De Castro (1890) and Valmaggi (1899).

records.title: Salvator Rosa Improvising
records.description:
An interior. Three people seated in the centre and to the left- two girls and a cavalier. On the right stands the painter and musician holding a lute in profile left. Signed " P. Bouvier, 1877. Milano."

 Exhibited at Milan in the Triennial Exhibition, 1876.  There awarded the Humberto Prize. An example of XIXth Century genre that was in great measure inspired by Meissonier, whose success in 1855, at the French Exhibition, was consummate.  This kind of modern genre is yet among the most popular forms of pictures. Salvator Rosa, whose romantic career was equalled by his vogue as a painter, was at first unable to make his mark as an artist. He therefore in 1639 abandoned painting and came out as a poet, singer, and actor. The nature of his improvisation in the above picture can be guessed from the varying expressions of his audience.

records.title: The Favourite
records.catalog_note: Casado, a man of patrician family, was born in Valencia; he studied in San Fernandos and Madrid. In 1860 he won the Prix de Rome, and first class medals in Madrid in 1862-64 and 1881. He was Director of the Spanish Academy and Court painter. He died 1895. He had the Cross of the Order of Isabel, given for his Bell of Huesca, now in the Modern Museum, Madrid.
records.description:
The interior of the harem. The favourite, a  white woman, reclines in the centre, naked to the waist.  Round her waist a chalk-white drapery, contrasting with the rose-pearl flesh and the deep sea-blue robe covering her legs. Her left arm extended behind her on a turquoise-green silk shawl that contrasts with the rose-grey flesh and gold background. Behind the figure on the left a bronze-amber coloured hanging; to  he right white marble. Beneath the body and in the foreground deep mulberry colour, light indigo-blue and crimson. In the extreme left foreground is repeated the turquiose-green of the silk shawl. Flowers in a pot, right, in the background. Signed " Casado."

 A Spanish writer has mentioned this picture as " One of his latest works is one of the favourites of fiction; ' belle et nonchalante,' dirait le poete, ' inutile et dangereuse,' repondrait le philosophe." The picture is a study in the emotional value of colour, sweet and delicate and sensuous, like music of this kind. Other pictures by Casado are The Death of Ferdinand IV, Semiramis, Goya's Studio, Beheaded Arabs, In the Boudoir (1882), Temptation (1884), and Laura (1885).

records.title: A Woman with a Cat
records.catalog_note: Born at Senlis; pupil of Gros and Delaroche; in 1837 he won the Grand Prix de Rome. In 1847 he exhibited his enormous pseudo-classical Roman Orgy or Romans in the Decadence, now in the Luxembourg. This work gave a great impetus to the classic movement. Couture obtained many medals and the Legion of Honour; he decorated St. Eustache, Paris. Couture died 1879. He is represented at Boston and New York.
records.catalog_title: No. 73. A WOMAN WITH A CAT
records.description:
A half length, standing, the body turned left, the head facing the spectator. She wears a white cap and dress, and holds a tabby cat; background grey-brown deepening to dark brown. Signed " T. Couture."

 A picture of Couture's less academic style, and one in closer touch with more modern tendencies. Couture is notorious for his attempted suppression of Marnet's development. Manet, the great influence of the XIXth Century and one of its permanent masters, studied under Couture, who stood in the ranks of the Classicists. Manet's tendency to revolt from semi-classic historical painting and to paint the world as he saw it disturbed Couture. But before such a picture as the above we might think it almost inexplicable that Couture should have found himself at variance with Manet's ambitions. Indeed, there is in this picture something of the Manet influence.
records.image_alt: A Woman with a Cat, by Couture, Thomas

records.description:
The interior of the Pope's cabinet in the Vatican.  Julius II seated in the right centre, full face, in crimson cape and cap, and with his feet on a crimson cushion. Cardinal Bembo stands in the centre, profile left, his hat under his arm. Raphael stands on the left, profile right, by his unfinished portrait of the Pope. Behind him a pale blue hanging.
 Signed " Guerra."

 Painted in Rome 1877-78. When Julius II was sitting to Raphael (the portrait painted 1510 is now in the Pitti Gallery, Florence, and repetitions are in various galleries, among them the National Gallery, London)
 Cardinal Bembo was admitted to meet the young painter, whose fame was at its height.

 When the picture above described was painted in 1877 the papal rooms in the Vatican remained much as they were in 1510; the chair, foot cushion, tapestries, &c., being unchanged.

records.catalog_note: Born at Newtown, Penn.; educated in Philadelphia and at the National Academy. Studied in Paris under Couture, painted portraits. Was in Europe from 1845-1849. Elected N.A. 1851; lived in New York and Trenton Falls. Died 1890.

records.title: A glass with the squire
records.catalog_note: Studied in Dusseldorf (1848-51). Painted The Old Kentucky Home (1867), The Old Stage Coach (1871), Milton dictating to his Daughters (1875). Eastman Johnson's portraits are well known.
records.catalog_title: No. 91. A GLASS WITH THE SQUIRE
records.description:
A farmer in a black boxer hat and bottle-green coat standing on the left raising his glass to the squire, who stands facing him on the right. Between them in the centre a Sheraton sideboard and a cellarette on the top, open, showing five decanters and the peacock-blue lining. A map inscribed "Nantucket " and a wax taper holder on the white wall to the left. Signed " E. Johnson, 1880."

 An intimate study of character and type. In conception and treatment this picture anticipates the recent English genre school by about twenty years. In subject this is a typical scene of New England life, in the middle of the XIXth Century. The squire was usually the judge or attorney who, living in a village, would purchase his wood and hay from his farmer neighbours. It was the custom in such cases to drink a glass, usually of " old Medford," or, as may be inferred from the glasses in this picture, of some more aristocratic wine. A Captain Baxter, an old shipowner, posed for Johnson frequently; he figures in Embers. It is he who is the squire in the above, and one John Fealey, an Irishman, is the farmer.
records.references:
Baur, John I M. An American Genre Painter Eastman Johnson 1824-1906, Brooklyn Museum, 1940. number 61, plate XXVI;

 Hawkins Scrapbook 'Newspaper Cuttings Personal, p.93: Prov. Sunday Journal, 30 June 1907: '...one of Eastman Johnson's very best. It is a finished picture , with every detail wrought clearly and affectionately...The squire's face, especially, is a triumph of American portraiture. Gen. Hawkins, it is understood, secured this admirable work after many years of unsuccessful effort."

records.title: Merveilleuses Sous le Directoire
records.catalog_note:
Born in Ghent, trained under Gerome in Paris. Awarded a third class Medal in the Paris Salon 1874.  He lived in Paris. His death by suicide occurred in 1892. Among his pictures, all of which dealt with costume genre, are Incroyables (1870), Vanderbilt Coll., New York; Une Dispute (1872), W. Rockefeller
 Coll.; Coast of Scheveningen (1875), Corcoran Coll., Baltimore; Une Marriage sous le Directoire and Automme dans les Tuileries.
records.description:
A scene in the Tuileries or Luxembourg Gardens in the Directoire. A flight of steps across the foreground. At the top, about to descend, a lady in white, a fan in her left hand, looking to the right, where stands a dandy, holding a cane and looking round at une Merveilleuse. Behind, to left and right, groups promenading under the trees or seated criticising. Two sparrows flying down the steps. Signed " F. H. Kaemmerer."

 Dutch genre of the XIXth century dealing with the interesting period and costume of the French Directoire and Empire. Kaemmerer, who is represented in American Collections and in the Stedelijk Museum, Amsterdam, had a considerable vogue. His art to some extent corresponds with the work produced in England by the late followers of the Pre-Raphaelite movement, such as Marcus Stone, R.A. The above picture is alluded to in Bryan's Dictionary- Merveilleuses sous le Directoire and Une Dispute (now in Mr. W. Rockefeller's Collection) " are good examples of his style; indeed it was they who (sic) definitely established his reputation."
records.image_alt: Merveilleuses Sous le Directoire, by Kaemmerer, Frederik Hendrik

records.title: Reverie
records.description:
A woman dressed in white, facing profile left, leaning back in a green wooden chair and seen at three-quarters left. Her left hand lies in her lap her right on an open book on a little table beside her. There, too, are a yellow rose and rose dore covering. Pale background. Signed " Louis Antoine Leclercq."

 Painted in the Whistler tradition; a study of " values," or gently contrasting tone and colour. In motif the works of this School are as different as possible from the picture by Kaemmerer, for example. While the latter primarily depends for its attractiveness on something approaching anecdote, or irrelevant interest such as the costume of such and such a period, the Impressionists of the Manet and Whistler School entirely rely upon qualities exclusively proper to painting, i.e. colour, tone relations, and the expression of unposed life. Thus they are nearer to the older painters such as Rembrandt and Velazquez, who always approached their subject from the standpoint of pictorial properties or conditions.  Music affords the most lucid parallel. Music which attempted to introduce a picturesque or anecdotic element (such as bellringing, bird-whistling, clappers that imitate a horse's trotting, or the human voice) would be departing from the zone proper to music. It is thus with anecdotic painting.

records.description:
A North Brabant girl standing full face full length in the centre. She wears a grey willow-green dress and red-sienna cape; her bag of clear cloisonne-blue hangs from her arm. Her white Dutch cap is crowned with pink flowers. Behind her head a Dutch conventional landscape picture; below, a warm violet-grey wall. At her feet a smoke-grey cat. Signed " Gari Melchers."

records.title: Blanche of Navarre Imprisoned in the Chateau d'Orthez
records.catalog_title: No. 101. BLANCHE OF NAVARRE IMPRISONED IN THE CHATEAU D'ORTHEZ
records.description:
Blanche, imprisoned by her father, John of Aragon, is represented seated, almost full length, in her cell. Ghostly harpy hands on the left and demons behind threaten her. In the right foreground an enormous book. Signed " A. Plauzeau."

 Blanche of Navarre, daughter of John of Aragon, was married to Henry IV, called the Impotent, of Castille. She separated from him in 1453 by special dispensation and returned to her father's house. There she became the object of her stepmother's persecution. Nominated as successor to the Crown of Navarre, on her brother's death she was handed over by her father in 1461 to the mercies of her younger sister, the Comtesse de Foix. Escaping from her guard she fled for protection to her husband, Henry of Castille, whom she had divorced. But she was recaptured and immured in the Chateau d'Orthez, and there tortured by apparitions engineered by her father. This, however, did not satisfy her sister, the Comtesse de Foix, who had her poisoned by a waiting-maid.
records.references: Hawkins Scrapbook 'Newspaper Cuttings Personal' p.93: Providence Sunday Journal, 23 June 1907.

records.title: Poland Partitioned
records.description:
In the left centre Poland, a woman stripped and bound hand and foot, lies fainting, her hands tied up above her head to a wayside shrine. An eagle gripping her left arm is making to rend her, two others approach from the left. A German soldier stands on guard behind her. To the right children are borne away in Russian waggons, in a line reaching to the dark storm-obscured horizon. The devouring eagle's pinion casts the shadow of a cross across the foreground. Signed " A. Plauzeau."

 An allegory of the fate of Poland- the ultimate annihilation of Poland as a unit. The sentinel in the background is on duty to prevent any intervention on behalf of the helpless woman.

 This picture and the above, No. 101, depend for their appeal on a presupposed knowledge of historical matter.

records.title: Scenes from the Life of Christ
records.references:
Anne van Buren, visiting Professor in Art History describes the woodcuts as Dutch (probably Utrecht) circa 1450.

 1.  Nativity is by a follower of the Master of Catherine of Cleves.
 2-5, Adoration of the Magi, Christ before Pilate, Flagellation, Entombment
 All four by a group of artist that worked for Otto van Mordrecht (Catalogue of Dutch miniatures, Morgan Library).   Differences in palette and brushwork are quite notable, bu the two artists were working in association.  (Note shed in scenes 1 and 2.)  All from a book of hours.

 The date of 1440-50 is based on the depth , lack of smooth flow into the distance, and costume.
